paragraphs.heading: The floor of the oceans
paragraphs.text: Oceanic crust is the top layer of the ocean parts of tectonic plates. It rests on the rigid top layer of the mantle, and the two together form the oceanic lithosphere. It is made mainly of mafic rock, also called sima, which is rich in iron and magnesium. It is thinner than continental crust, usually under 10 km, but denser, about 3.0 grams per cubic centimeter against about 2.7.

paragraphs.heading: Made at mid-ocean ridges
paragraphs.text: New oceanic crust forms all the time at mid-ocean ridges. As plates pull apart there, magma rises into the upper mantle and crust. The top of the crust is magma from the mantle that has cooled. Most eruptions happen at these ridges, but some come from scattered hotspots and from rare, powerful flood basalt eruptions.

paragraphs.heading: Three layers
paragraphs.text: Oceanic crust is much simpler than continental crust and usually splits into three layers. Layer 1, about 0.4 km thick on average, is loose or partly hardened sediment, thin or absent near the ridges and thicker farther away. Layer 2 has an upper part about 0.5 km thick of basalt, often as pillow basalt, over a part about 1.5 km thick made of diabase dikes. Layer 3 is coarse-grained gabbro and ultramafic rocks that formed as magma cooled slowly underground. At almost 5 km thick, it holds over two-thirds of the crust's volume.

paragraphs.heading: Why most of it is the same thickness
paragraphs.text: As mantle rock rises, the pressure on it drops and it begins to melt. How much melt forms depends only on the mantle's temperature as it rises, so most oceanic crust is about 7 km thick, give or take 1 km. Very slow ridges such as the Gakkel Ridge under the Arctic Ocean make thinner crust, 4 to 5 km. Above plumes the mantle is hotter, so it melts more and makes thicker crust; Iceland's is about 20 km.

paragraphs.heading: Older with distance
paragraphs.text: As plates carry new rock away from a ridge, it cools and sediment slowly piles up on it. So the youngest ocean rocks sit at the ridges, and the rocks get steadily older the farther away they are. The crust's age can even be used to estimate how thick the lithosphere beneath it is, since older crust has a thicker layer of mantle lithosphere under it.

paragraphs.heading: Recycled into the mantle
paragraphs.text: Oceanic lithosphere sinks back into the mantle, or subducts, at convergent boundaries. These can lie between two ocean plates or between an ocean plate and a continent. When ocean meets continent, the ocean side always sinks, because continental lithosphere is less dense. This steady loss of older ocean floor means oceanic crust is rarely more than 200 million years old.

paragraphs.heading: How we know what is down there
paragraphs.text: No one has yet drilled through a complete section of oceanic crust. Geologists instead study ophiolites, slices of ocean crust pushed up onto continents and preserved there. They also compare seismic data with lab measurements of wave speeds in known rocks, and they study samples gathered by submersibles, dredging and drilling.
